title: Chapter 27 — Knights and Squires
paragraphs: Stubb was the second mate, a native of Cape Cod, and therefore known as a Cape Cod man. He was a happy-go-lucky type — neither cowardly nor heroic — taking dangers as they came with an air of indifference. In the most critical moment of the chase, he worked away as calmly as a carpenter hired by the year. Good-humored, easy, and carefree, he ran his whale-boat as if the most deadly encounter were just a dinner party and his crew the invited guests. He was as particular about the comfortable arrangement of his part of the boat as an old stagecoach driver is about the coziness of his seat. When close to the whale, in the very death grip of the fight, he handled his merciless lance coolly and casually, like a whistling handyman tapping his hammer. He would hum his old tunes while fighting flank to flank with the most enraged beast. Long experience had, for Stubb, converted the jaws of death into a comfortable chair. What he thought about death itself, there's no telling. Whether he ever thought about it at all was debatable. But if he did happen to turn his mind that way after a good dinner, no doubt, like a sensible sailor, he took it as a sort of call of the watch — an order to tumble up on deck and get busy with something he'd learn about when he obeyed the order, and not before.

What helped make Stubb such an easygoing, fearless man, so cheerfully carrying the burden of life in a world full of solemn worriers bent double under their loads — what contributed to his almost irreverent good humor — that must have been his pipe. For like his nose, his short black little pipe was one of the permanent features of his face. You'd have sooner expected him to climb out of his bunk without his nose than without his pipe. He kept a whole row of them, pre-loaded, in a rack within easy reach. Whenever he turned in, he smoked them all in succession, lighting each from the last until they were done, then reloading them all for next time. When Stubb got dressed, instead of putting his legs into his trousers first, he put his pipe into his mouth.

I say this constant smoking must have been one cause, at least, of his peculiar temperament. For everyone knows that the earthly air, whether on land or sea, is terribly infected with the nameless miseries of the countless people who have died breathing it. And just as during a cholera outbreak some people walk around pressing camphor-soaked handkerchiefs to their mouths, so too, against all mortal troubles, Stubb's tobacco smoke may have served as a kind of disinfectant.

The third mate was Flask, a native of Tisbury on Martha's Vineyard. A short, stocky, ruddy young fellow, tremendously combative when it came to whales. He somehow seemed to believe that the great creatures had personally and hereditably insulted him, and therefore it was a point of honor to destroy them whenever he found them. He had so completely lost all sense of reverence for the many marvels of their majestic size and mysterious ways, and was so utterly deaf to any possibility of danger from them, that in his humble opinion a whale was nothing but a species of oversized mouse — or at least a water rat — requiring only a little cleverness and some time and effort to kill and boil. This ignorant, unconscious fearlessness made him playful about whales. He hunted them for the fun of it. A three-year voyage around Cape Horn was just a long-running joke. As a carpenter's nails are divided into wrought nails and cut nails, so mankind can be similarly divided. Little Flask was one of the wrought ones — made to grip tight and last long. They called him King-Post aboard the Pequod, because in shape he resembled the short, square timber known by that name in Arctic whalers, which, by means of many radiating side timbers, braces the ship against the battering ice.

Now these three mates — Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask — were important men. By universal tradition, they commanded three of the Pequod's boats as headsmen. In the grand battle formation in which Captain Ahab would likely arrange his forces to descend on the whales, these three headsmen were like company captains. Or, armed with their long, keen whaling lances, they were a chosen trio of lancers, just as the harpooners were throwers of javelins.

And since in this famous fishery, each mate or headsman, like a Gothic knight of old, is always accompanied by his boat-steerer or harpooner — who in certain tight spots provides him with a fresh lance when the first one has been bent or broken in the attack — and since a close friendship generally exists between the two, it is fitting that we record here who the Pequod's harpooners were and which headsman each of them served.
First was Queequeg, whom Starbuck, the chief mate, had chosen as his squire. But Queequeg is already known to us.

Next was Tashtego, a pure-blooded Indian from Gay Head, the westernmost point of Martha's Vineyard, where the last remnant of a Native village still exists — a community that has long supplied neighboring Nantucket with many of its boldest harpooners. In the fishery, they usually go by the general name of Gay-Headers. Tashtego's long, lean, jet-black hair, his high cheekbones, and his dark, rounded eyes — large like an Oriental's but with an Antarctic glitter — all proclaimed him the inheritor of the pure blood of those proud warrior-hunters who, bow in hand, had once ranged the ancient forests of the mainland in pursuit of the great New England moose. But no longer tracking wild beasts through the woods, Tashtego now hunted in the wake of the great whales of the sea. The unerring harpoon of the son had fittingly replaced the infallible arrow of his ancestors. Looking at the tawny muscle of his lithe, snake-like limbs, you could almost credit the superstitions of the early Puritans and half-believe this wild Indian to be a son of the Prince of the Powers of the Air. Tashtego was Stubb's squire.

Third among the harpooners was Daggoo, a gigantic, coal-black African, with a lion-like stride — a magnificent sight to behold. From his ears hung two golden hoops so large that the sailors called them ring-bolts and joked about tying the topsail ropes to them. In his youth, Daggoo had voluntarily signed aboard a whaler anchored in a lonely bay on his native coast. Having never been anywhere in the world except Africa, Nantucket, and the remote ports most visited by whalemen — and having lived for years the bold life of the fishery on ships whose owners were unusually particular about their crews — Daggoo retained all his untamed virtues. Standing straight as a giraffe, he moved about the decks in all the majesty of six feet five in his socks. There was a physical humility in looking up at him. A white man standing before him seemed like a white flag come to beg a truce from a fortress. Curiously, this magnificent Daggoo was the squire of little Flask, who looked like a chess piece beside him. As for the rest of the Pequod's crew, it should be said that today, not one in two of the many thousands of common sailors in the American whale fishery are American-born, though nearly all the officers are. It's the same with the American whale fishery as with the American army, navy, and merchant marine, and the workers who built the American canals and railroads. The same, I say, because in all these cases native Americans generously supply the brains, while the rest of the world generously supplies the muscle. Many of these whaling sailors come from the Azores, where outbound Nantucket whalers frequently stop to add to their crews from the hardy islanders. Similarly, Greenland whalers sailing out of Hull or London stop at the Shetland Islands to pick up their full complement and drop them off again on the way home. Why it is, there's no telling, but islanders seem to make the best whalemen. They were nearly all islanders on the Pequod — Isolatoes, as I call them, not acknowledging the common continent of mankind, but each living on a separate continent of his own. Yet now, joined along one keel, what a crew these Isolatoes made! A delegation from all the islands of the sea and all the ends of the earth, accompanying old Ahab on the Pequod to present the world's grievances before that bar from which not many of them would ever return. Black little Pip — he never did. Oh no, he went before. Poor Alabama boy! On the grim Pequod's forecastle, you shall soon see him beating his tambourine — a prelude to the eternal time when, summoned to the great quarter-deck on high, he was told to join the angels and beat his tambourine in glory. Called a coward here, hailed a hero there!
